metaTitle: How to Build a Retirement Plan: 8 Steps to Take Today
metaDescription: Learn how to build a retirement plan in eight clear steps. Calculate your target savings, automate contributions, and set up your investment strategy.
h1: How to Build a Retirement Plan in 8 Steps
subtitle: An ordered checklist to calculate your target nest egg, automate savings, and set up your investments.
introText:
Learning how to build a retirement plan comes down to an orderly sequence: calculate your future living costs, set a lump-sum target, and automate monthly deposits into tax-sheltered investment accounts. At ModernWallet, we help readers replace vague savings goals with clear steps that turn income into long-term financial security.

Guesswork rarely builds wealth. Starting without a structured process leaves you unsure whether your monthly savings will cover your future bills. Following a simple retirement plan checklist gives you an immediate roadmap to invest consistently and track your progress over time.

sections.heading: Step 1: Picture What Retirement Looks Like for You
sections.content:
Your target retirement spending begins with the day-to-day lifestyle choices you expect to make once you leave full-time employment. Before you calculate any financial figures, work through the initial retirement planning steps of mapping out how you intend to spend your time and where you want to live. A retirement focused on international travel and dining out requires a much larger portfolio than one centered on gardening and spending time with local family.

Consider how your housing arrangements will look during your retirement years. Some people plan to stay in their existing home, while others prefer to downsize or relocate to an area with lower property taxes. Deciding whether you will enter retirement with a paid-off mortgage or a continuing housing payment fundamentally alters your cash flow needs.

Decide whether your retirement includes any ongoing earned income. Many retirees transition gradually by working twenty hours per week in consulting or pursuing passion projects. Even modest part-time earnings of $15,000 per year cut a real chunk off the amount your investment portfolio must generate each month.

sections.heading: Step 2: Pick a Target Retirement Age
sections.content:
Selecting your target retirement age establishes your accumulation timeline and determines the health insurance and account withdrawal rules that govern your savings. Your target age dictates how many years remain for your portfolio to compound. It also sets the financial bridge you must fund if you stop working before standard safety nets activate.

Health care is often the largest financial hurdle for individuals retiring before age 65. Traditional [Medicare](https://www.medicare.gov/) eligibility begins at age 65, which means leaving the workforce early requires funding private coverage. You must budget for private health policies, use COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) continuation coverage, or join a spouse's workplace plan to cover medical care during the gap years.

Age also dictates how easily you can access your accumulated retirement savings without penalties. Under federal rules, early distributions from a traditional 401(k) or Individual Retirement Account (IRA) prior to age 59½ trigger a 10% penalty alongside ordinary income tax. Our guide on [how to withdraw from a 401(k)](/guides/how-to-withdraw-from-401k/) explains the narrow exceptions to this penalty and outlines how to plan early withdrawals cleanly.

sections.heading: Step 3: Estimate What That Lifestyle Costs Each Year
sections.content:
A reliable estimate of annual retirement expenses starts by calculating baseline living costs rather than guessing an arbitrary number. Review your current household budget to identify expenses that will disappear when you stop working, such as commuting costs, professional wardrobes, and payroll taxes. At the same time, account for categories that will likely increase, including personal travel, entertainment, and out-of-pocket health care deductibles.

According to the [U.S. Department of Labor (DOL)](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/ebsa/about-ebsa/our-activities/resource-center/publications/what-you-should-know-about-your-retirement-plan), most retirees need roughly 70% to 90% of their pre-retirement income to maintain their standard of living. This guideline serves as an initial benchmark, but your personal spending plan determines your actual cash needs. Someone who enters retirement debt-free with modest local interests may thrive on 60% of their prior income, while someone planning extensive overseas travel may require 95%.

Organize your anticipated costs into nondiscretionary survival expenses and flexible lifestyle choices. Core costs include housing, groceries, utilities, and insurance premiums, while discretionary costs cover hobbies and dining out. Run your numbers through our [retirement savings calculator](/retirement/retirement-savings-calculator/) to see how small adjustments to your yearly spending target alter your overall plan.

sections.heading: Step 4: How to Build a Retirement Plan Target from Annual Expenses
sections.content:
Multiplying your estimated annual living expenses by 25 converts your yearly budget into a clear total savings target. For instance, if your baseline budget requires $60,000 per year from your investments, multiplying that figure by 25 produces a target portfolio of $1,500,000. This calculation matches the mathematics behind the four percent initial withdrawal rule, which assumes a balanced portfolio can sustain annual distributions adjusted for inflation over a thirty-year retirement.

Guaranteed retirement income sources reduce the net dollar amount your portfolio must generate on its own. If you anticipate receiving $20,000 annually from Social Security, your portfolio only needs to cover the remaining $40,000 of a $60,000 budget. Multiplying $40,000 by 25 drops your required nest egg target from $1,500,000 down to $1,000,000.

Our recommendation to target a 25x nest egg would change if you hold a defined-benefit pension or commercial real estate that produces dependable cash flow. Reliable non-portfolio income allows you to retire on a smaller liquid balance. To see how different milestones work in practice, explore our guides on [how to become a 401(k) millionaire](/guides/how-to-become-a-401k-millionaire/) and [how to retire with $1 million](/guides/how-to-retire-with-1-million/).

sections.heading: Step 5: Automate Savings Contributions and Schedule Annual Increases
sections.content:
Automating your payroll deductions removes willpower from the equation and guarantees that your retirement accounts receive funding every single pay period. Setting up automatic transfers directly from your paycheck into a workplace retirement plan ensures you invest before discretionary spending occurs. Relying on manual end-of-month bank transfers often fails because everyday expenses gradually absorb leftover cash.

Pair your automated deductions with a scheduled annual contribution increase to accelerate wealth accumulation over time. Many employer plans feature an automatic escalation setting that raises your savings rate by one or two percentage points each year. Coordinating this automated bump with your annual compensation review allows you to save more money without feeling a pinch in your take-home pay.

This linear savings checklist is not for people currently carrying high-interest consumer debt. If you owe balances on credit cards charging double-digit interest rates, eliminate those debts before investing money beyond your employer matching threshold. Once you eliminate toxic consumer debt, redirect those freed-up cash payments directly into your automated retirement schedule.

sections.heading: Step 6: Invest Your Savings Based on Your Timeline
sections.content:
Aligning your investment asset allocation with your retirement timeline protects your purchasing power while keeping downside market volatility manageable. Younger savers with decades ahead of them can hold a high proportion of equities to outpace inflation and maximize compound growth. As you enter the decade preceding your target retirement date, shifting a portion of your portfolio into fixed-income bonds helps protect your accumulated principal.

Target-date index funds offer an efficient, hands-off mechanism to manage this portfolio glide path automatically. These funds hold a diversified blend of stocks and bonds, gradually shifting toward conservative assets as your target year nears. This hands-off structure removes the stress of picking individual stocks.

Investors who prefer a customized portfolio can construct a simple three-fund portfolio using broad market index funds. This structure combines a total domestic stock market index, a total international stock index, and a total bond market index. To learn more about selecting low-cost funds and structuring your portfolio, explore our comprehensive [investing hub](/investing/).

sections.heading: Step 7: Use Every Year of Tax-Advantaged Room Before It Resets
sections.content:
Tax-advantaged contribution limits reset on the first day of each calendar year, meaning any unused contribution room disappears forever once the annual deadline passes. Missing a year of contributions represents lost tax-deferred growth that you can never recover in future tax years. Structuring your monthly budget to capture as much tax-advantaged capacity as possible substantially lowers your lifetime tax burden.

For 2026, the [Internal Revenue Service (IRS)](https://www.irs.gov/newsroom/401k-limit-increases-to-24500-for-2026-ira-limit-increases-to-7500) sets the employee 401(k) contribution limit at $24,500. Workers age 50 and older can add an $8,000 catch-up contribution. Under SECURE 2.0, individuals ages 60 to 63 qualify for a higher catch-up limit of $11,250.

Individual Retirement Accounts provide another valuable layer of tax-advantaged savings with a 2026 combined contribution ceiling of $7,500. You can review all current thresholds and eligibility parameters in our detailed guide to [401(k) contribution limits for 2026](/guides/401k-contribution-limits-2026/). Coordinating both workplace accounts and IRAs ensures you shelter maximum income from current or future income taxes.

sections.heading: Step 8: Action Steps on How to Build a Retirement Plan This Week
sections.content:
Starting your retirement savings today provides a decisive compounding advantage over waiting for the perfect financial moment. Delaying the start of your retirement savings by roughly a decade typically means needing two to three times the monthly contribution to reach the exact same target balance. You can see the math behind this compounding penalty in our analysis of [retirement planning mistakes to avoid](/guides/retirement-planning-mistakes-to-avoid/).

Do not let uncertainty about future tax brackets or investment choices stall your progress. Working through a retirement plan checklist in your twenties or thirties outperforms an elaborate strategy launched late in your career. You can easily adjust contribution rates, target dates, and asset allocations as your household income and life circumstances evolve over time.

Take one concrete action this week to establish your financial trajectory. Use our free [retirement calculator](/retirement/) to run your baseline numbers with a rough spending estimate, then set up an initial payroll deduction to get moving. Running your numbers now provides the exact starting point you need to learn how to build a retirement plan that fits your monthly budget.

faqItems.question: What is the first step in building a retirement plan?
faqItems.answer: The first step is deciding what you want your everyday life to look like in retirement. Map out your expected housing, travel, and lifestyle choices before running any financial calculations. These qualitative decisions determine your future living expenses, which form the baseline for your savings target.

faqItems.question: How do I figure out how much money I will need to retire?
faqItems.answer: Multiply your expected annual retirement expenses by 25 to establish your total savings target. This rule of thumb reflects the 4% withdrawal guideline, which assumes a balanced portfolio can support distributions over a thirty-year retirement. For example, if you need your portfolio to cover $50,000 each year, your baseline savings goal is $1,250,000.

faqItems.question: What if I am starting a retirement plan late, in my 40s or 50s?
faqItems.answer: Starting late requires maximizing tax-advantaged catch-up contributions and focusing on high savings rates. For 2026, savers age 50 and older can contribute an extra $8,000 to a 401(k), while those ages 60 to 63 can add $11,250 under SECURE 2.0. Cutting discretionary spending and extending your working career by even two or three years also closes much of the savings gap.

faqItems.question: Do I need a financial advisor to build a retirement plan?
faqItems.answer: You do not need a financial advisor to build an effective initial retirement plan. Most individuals can successfully plan by using broad target-date index funds and automated contributions in employer-sponsored accounts. An advisor can provide value later when navigating complex estate planning, tax-location strategies, or irregular business income.

faqItems.question: How often should I revisit my retirement plan once it is built?
faqItems.answer: Review your retirement plan once every year or whenever you experience a major life event. An annual checkup allows you to increase contribution percentages, rebalance your portfolio back to target asset weights, and incorporate salary raises. Major life transitions such as marriage, buying a home, or changing employers also warrant an immediate plan review.
